questions.questionText: Extract B (lines 6–7) states: ‘Some analysts hope that, before long, the currency will start to appreciate which could help Norway reduce inflation.’ With the help of a suitable diagram, explain how an appreciation of the krone could help Norway reduce inflation.
In a particular year, the rate of inflation in an economy was 2% and real national income rose by 6%. What was the approximate increase in the economy’s nominal national income in that year?
Explain how supply-side policies can help to achieve a low, stable rate of inflation.
Evaluate the view that a low rate of inflation is always beneficial for a country’s macroeconomic performance.

Table 4 shows the index of consumer prices and the unemployment rate for an economy. The data is for the end of each quarter in a particular year. The index of consumer prices for the final quarter of the previous year was 120.9. According to the data, it can be concluded that
options: prices were lower at the start of the year and employment was lower at the end of the year.
the quarterly inflation rate fluctuated whilst the unemployment rate increased throughout the year.
the relationship between the change in the inflation and unemployment rates was positive in each quarter.
there was an inverse relationship between prices and unemployment in each quarter.

questions.questionText: All other things being equal, which one of the following is most likely to be a consequence of inflation in the UK?
options: The amounts outstanding on households’ existing mortgages will fall in real terms
The nominal value of people’s incomes before tax will fall
The price of all goods and services sold in the UK will increase
The real value of the money deposited in commercial banks will increase

questions.questionText: Extract C (lines 4–5) states ‘Energy and food bills had risen dramatically due to shocks to the economy, such as labour shortages, a depreciation of the pound…’ With the help of a diagram, explain how a depreciation of the pound may cause inflation.
Disinflation exists when
options: an economy experiences a fall in the cost of living.
deflation has occurred for two or more successive quarters.
nominal incomes are rising more slowly than prices.
the price level is rising less quickly than previously.

questions.questionText: Assess whether an increase in the money supply is always damaging for an economy.

Country W is operating at its normal capacity level of output. When one of its trading partners experiences economic growth, this leads to a rise in demand for Country W’s exports. All other things being equal, what is the most likely consequence of this for Country W?
options: A fall in employment and a reduction in cost-push inflation
A negative output gap and a period of disinflation
A positive output gap and an increase in demand-pull inflation
An increase in unemployment and a fall in the price level

questions.questionText: Which one of the following functions of money is likely to be most effective during a period of deflation?
options: Measure of value
Standard of deferred payment
Store of value
Unit of account

questions.questionText: Table 9 shows the price index for an economy at the end of each of the years from 2019 to 2023. In which year did the economy experience disinflation?
In which one of the following situations is an increase in aggregate demand most likely to result in higher inflation?
options: Household savings are increasing
Mortgage interest rates are high
Resources are fully employed
Unemployment is rising

questions.questionText: Table 1 shows the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for an economy over a period of time. Which one of the following can be concluded from Table 1?
options: The price of a representative basket of goods rose throughout the period.
The rate of inflation from 2011 to 2014 was the same as from 2014 to 2017.
The standard of living reached its highest level in 2020.
The value of money rose between 2008 and 2011.

questions.questionText: An economy is experiencing deflation and high employment. The most likely cause of this situation is a
options: deficit on the balance of payments.
government budget surplus.
negative demand-side shock.
positive supply-side shock.

questions.questionText: The quantity theory of money can be explained using Irving Fisher’s equation of exchange, MV=PQ. Monetarist economists believe that the theory helps to explain inflation because some parts of the equation are normally stable. Which parts of the equation do monetarist economists normally consider to be stable?
options: M and P
M and V
P and Q
V and Q

questions.questionText: Figure 4 shows a short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) and a long-run Phillips curve (LRPC). Government intervention moves the economy from position A to position B and then the economy moves from position B to position C. Which one of the following is most likely to explain the movement from position B to position C?
options: Demand for exports has risen as a result of the intervention
Economic agents have higher inflation expectations due to the intervention
The government cut taxes to reduce unemployment
The intervention has increased the natural rate of unemployment

questions.questionText: A deflationary policy is designed to
options: avoid deflation.
increase aggregate demand.
lead to deflation.
reduce aggregate demand.

questions.questionText: Nominal GDP for an economy fell from £318 billion to £310 billion. Average prices also fell over the same period. It can be concluded that
options: deflation resulted in a recession.
output fell, but by less than £8billion.
real GDP was lower at the end of the period.
real incomes may have risen or fallen.

questions.questionText: A government wanting to use monetary policy to reduce deflation could decrease the
options: exchange rate.
minimum wage.
money supply.
rate of indirect tax.

questions.questionText: In an economy, an index showing the change in the money supply multiplied by the velocity of circulation increases from 100 to 115.5. At the same time, the final output produced by the economy increases from 100 to 110. According to Fisher’s equation of exchange, the price level will increase by
Us ing th e data in Extract D (Figure 4), calculate South Korea’s rate of inflation for the year ended 31 December 2019. Give your answer to two decimal places.

Evaluate the possible impact on the cost of living and the standard of living in the UK of a sustained rise in the value of the pound sterling against other currencies, such as the euro and the US dollar.

Table 1 contains data for the rates of growth of nominal and real GDP and the rate of inflation for an economy in a given year. Which one of the following combinations, A, B, C or D, shows the correct relationship between the three variables?

Table 2 shows the inflation rate and the rate of growth of the money supply for an economy between 2016 and 2019. From the data in Table 2 it may be concluded that, all other things being equal, there was
options: a fall in the value of money throughout the entire period.
a policy of quantitative easing in operation throughout the entire period.
an inverse relationship between inflation and the rate of growth of the money supply.
continuous disinflation throughout the entire period.

questions.questionText: Which one of the following statements about the consumer price index (CPI) is correct?
options: A fall in the CPI means that the real value of money is falling
An increase in the CPI means that the rate of inflation is rising
The CPI measures changes in the prices of goods and services bought by households
The weights used in the CPI reflect changes in the quality of goods and services

questions.questionText: An economy is experiencing short-run economic growth accompanied by falling unemployment. This is due to rising aggregate demand following the introduction of an expansionary fiscal policy. Which one of the following is most likely to help the economy avoid rising inflation?
options: A fall in the exchange rate and falling productivity
A fall in the exchange rate and rising productivity
A rise in the exchange rate and falling productivity
A rise in the exchange rate and rising productivity

questions.questionText: Figure 3 shows an economy’s aggregate demand (AD) and short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves. The initial equilibrium price level is at OP1. Which one of the following is most likely to be responsible for both the cost–push and demand-pull inflationary pressures that raise the price level to OP2?
options: A fall in interest rates
A fall in the exchange rate
A rise in direct taxes
A rise in indirect taxes

questions.questionText: Output of the UK economy is at the normal capacity level and the Bank of England decides to implement measures to restrict the supply of credit to households. The most likely reason for this policy is that
options: earnings are increasing fast.
house prices are falling.
productivity is growing more quickly.
the exchange rate is appreciating.

questions.questionText: Explain the main causes of a rise in inflation.
Evaluate the view that inflation is always preferable to deflation.
Which one of the following sets of circumstances is most likely, other things remaining the same, to lead to demand-pull and cost-push inflation in an economy?
options: A depreciation in the exchange rate, and a reduction in the government’s budget surplus
Labour productivity growth in the economy accelerates, and interest rates fall
The minimum wage is increased, and business confidence in the economy falls
World demand for commodities increases, and the economy’s trade surplus becomes smaller

questions.questionText: The table below contains selected data on a country’s macroeconomic performance over a 20 year period. All other things being equal, which one of the following, A, B, C or D, can be inferred from the above data?
options: The natural rate of unemployment is falling
The price level is increasing more slowly
The volume of exports is increasing
There is an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation

questions.questionText: All other things being equal, if the velocity of circulation is constant, the quantity theory of money based on Fisher’s equation of exchange, MV=PQ, predicts that an x% increase in the money supply will always cause an x%
options: decrease in the rate of interest.
increase in nominal national income.
increase in real national income.
increase in the rate of economic growth.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the annual rate of inflation in the UK between 2011 and 2014. From the graph it can be concluded that between 2011 and 2014
options: real wages increased.
the price level was rising.
the real value of money increased.
the UK experienced deflation.

questions.questionText: The world market price of oil falls by 40 per cent. Other things remaining the same, the impact on the UK economy is most likely to be
options: an increase in aggregate demand and inflation.
deflation and lower output.
disinflation and higher output.
higher unemployment and inflation.

questions.questionText: The table below shows indices for real GDP and consumer prices in an economy over six quarters. During these six quarters the economy experienced
options: deflation and a recession.
disinflation when in recession.
disinflation when recovering from recession.
rising inflation when recovering from recession.

questions.questionText: Using the data in Extract D (Figure 3), calculate, to two decimal places, the mean inflation rate for Japan from 2010 to 2015.
Explain how the data in Extract D (Figure 4) show that Japan has been less successful than the UK in achieving a stable rate of economic growth.

Extract F (lines 19–20) states ‘What is not clear is what should be done if low inflation turns to bad deflation.’ Using the data in the extracts and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that monetary policy is the most effective way of tackling deflation in developed economies such as the UK and Japan.
The annual rate of change in the consumer prices index for an economy falls from 6% to 3%. All other things being equal, this economy is best described as
options: entering a positive output gap.
entering a recovery period.
experiencing deflation.
experiencing disinflation.

questions.questionText: All other things being equal, under which of the following circumstances is an economy most likely to experience deflation?
The table below shows the Consumer Prices Index for a country over a number of years. Which one of the following can be concluded from the table?
options: The country suffered disinflation in Year 5
The inflation rate was highest in Year 7
The only time the country suffered deflation was in Year 2
Real incomes fell between Year 1 and Year 7

questions.questionText: An economy is in macroeconomic equilibrium, producing at its normal capacity level of output. Without long-run economic growth, a persistent increase in aggregate demand is likely to lead to an increase in the level of
options: real GDP.
employment.
productivity.
prices.
